migrationNotes: Spine: follow a bag of shopping. Put a number on the pull of gravity, find what holds it up at rest, carry it in a lift going up and down, then take it to the Moon.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): phys-weight-and-support-1 (a second W = mg item) and -2 (mass versus weight, covered by the transfer). Skill check is now -5, -3 and check-3; -6 moved into the lesson as a practice screen.

lesson.title: Weight and support

steps.headline: The pull of gravity on a bag

lead.text: Start with the bag on its own. Gravity pulls on every kilogram of it with a force of about 10 N, so a 2 kg bag is pulled down with 20 N and a 5 kg bag with 50 N. The pull of gravity on an object is called its weight. It grows in step with the mass, so the weight is the mass times the pull on one kilogram.

Here g is 10 N for every kilogram, which is the same number as the 10 m/s² of free fall, because 1 N is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons and it points down. Mass is measured in kilograms.

afterFigure.text: This also explains the end of the lesson on falling. A freely falling object has only its weight acting on it, so the second law gives it an acceleration of W ÷ m = mg ÷ m = g. The mass cancels, and every object in free fall has the same acceleration.

lead.text: Each kilogram of the bag is pulled down by the same amount.

Put the 5 kg bag on a table. Its weight is still 50 N, pulling down. If that were the only force on it, the net force would point down and the bag would accelerate down through the table. It does not, so something is pushing up. The table is, and the upward push of a surface on whatever rests on it is called the support force.

The bag is at rest. Its acceleration is zero, and by the second law the net force on it is zero as well. The upward support force and the downward weight have to be equal and opposite, which means the support force is mg. For the 5 kg bag that is 50 N. The table does not push with a fixed amount. It pushes as hard as it needs to until it breaks, and a heavier bag gets a harder push.

afterFigure.text: Take the table away and the support force goes with it. The weight is then the only force on the bag, which is free fall again.

lead.text: A shelf holds a box in the same way that the table held the bag.

steps.headline: Support in a lift that speeds up

lead.text: Now put the bag in a lift that is speeding up as it rises. The bag accelerates upward with the lift, so its acceleration is not zero and the net force on it cannot be zero either. The second law gives the size of that net force: the mass times the acceleration, pointing up.

Take up as positive. The support force pushes up and the weight pulls down, so the net force is the support force − mg. Setting that equal to ma gives the support force − mg = ma, and so the support force = m(g + a). The floor has to carry the weight and also supply the extra push ma that accelerates the bag. A 3 kg bag in a lift speeding up at 1 m/s² needs 3 × (10 + 1) = 33 N from the floor, which is 3 N more than at rest.

afterFigure.text: That extra push is why you feel heavier for the first moment of a ride up. The floor pushes harder on your feet than it does when the lift is standing still.

steps.headline: A 2 kg load is carried upward at 3 m/s² in a lift. Find the support force. Take g as 10 m/s².

workedSteps.text: The net upward force must give the acceleration.
The support force carries the weight and supplies the net force.

steps.headline: A 4 kg object is accelerated upward at 2 m/s². Find the support force with g = 10 m/s².

workedSteps.text: The extra force for the acceleration is ma.
Add them to find the support force.

steps.headline: Lifts that go down or move steadily

lead.text: Turn the lift round and the same equation still works. Only the sign of the acceleration changes. If the lift speeds up downward, a is negative, so m(g + a) is smaller than the weight. A 3 kg bag in a lift speeding up downward at 1 m/s² has a support force of 3 × (10 − 1) = 27 N. The floor pushes less hard, and the bag feels lighter.

What matters is the acceleration, and the direction of travel makes no difference. A lift going down at a steady 2 m/s has an acceleration of zero, so the support force equals the weight, as if the lift were standing still. The same holds for a lift going up at a steady speed. The support force differs from the weight only while the velocity is changing.

Push the idea to its limit. If a is −g, the equation gives zero. The floor stops pushing, and the bag falls freely with the lift. That is the weightless feeling of free fall, and it is what astronauts in orbit feel, since they are falling freely all the time.

3 kg bag, lift in free fall

lead.text: A box rides on a platform that is moving steadily downward.

steps.headline: Mass stays the same and weight does not

lead.text: Carry the bag to the Moon. Gravity there pulls on each kilogram with about 1.6 N, so g on the Moon is 1.6 N per kilogram against Earth's 10. The 5 kg bag weighs 5 × 1.6 = 8 N and is far easier to lift. It is the same bag with the same amount of matter in it, and its mass is still 5 kg.

Weight and mass are easy to mix up, because everyday language uses both for how heavy something is and on Earth they go together. They are different quantities. Mass, in kilograms, belongs to the object and is the same everywhere. Weight, in newtons, depends on the mass and on g, so it changes from place to place. The second law uses mass, which is why the bag is just as hard to start moving sideways on the Moon as on Earth.
Another planet has a different g from Earth's.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish mass, gravitational force and the force from a support.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Hold a bag of shopping at arm's length and your arm soon starts to ache. Put the bag on a table and the ache goes, though gravity is pulling on the bag exactly as before. The table is doing the job your arm was doing. The bag is not accelerating in either case, and the second law says what that means: the forces on it add up to zero, so something must be pushing up as hard as gravity pulls down.

Step into a lift with the bag and the story changes. When the lift sets off upward the bag feels heavier, and as the lift slows to a stop at the top it feels lighter. Your arm is a good instrument here, because it tells you how hard the bag has to be held up.
This lesson follows the bag. We put a number on the pull of gravity and work out what holds the bag up when everything is still. Then we see how the answer changes in a lift and on another world.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell mass from weight, and find the support force on an object at rest or accelerating.

recap.keyIdea: Weight is mg and changes with g; mass does not. A support force balances the weight at rest and exceeds it when the object accelerates upward.

blocks.text: You found that a 6 kg bag is pulled down with 60 N and that a 7 kg box needs 70 N from its shelf. You also found that a 4 kg object needs 48 N of support while it speeds up at 2 m/s², and that a 3 kg object weighs 12 N where g is 4 m/s².

recap.nextHook: The shelf pushes up on the box, so the box must push down on the shelf. Next we look at forces that come in pairs.

questions.prompt: An object has mass 3 kg where g = 10 m/s². Find the magnitude of its weight in newtons.
hints: Weight is a force produced by gravity.
Multiply mass by the stated gravitational acceleration.
Calculate 3 × 10.
questions.onCorrect: 30 N. Weight is mass times g: the gravitational force on the object.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass. Weight is a force: multiply the mass by g.
That adds the mass and g. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object moves to a location with smaller gravitational acceleration. What happens to its mass?
hints: Mass and weight measure different physical quantities.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the gravitational field changes weight; the object's mass remains 3 kg.

questions.onCorrect: It stays 3 kg. Mass belongs to the object; only the weight changes with the field.

misconceptions.feedback: Mass is the amount of matter, which does not change with place. Weight is what changes.
Weight is a force in newtons and mass is in kilograms. They are different quantities.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object rests on a horizontal support. Only its weight and the upward support force act, with g = 10 m/s². Find the support force in newtons.
hints: At rest, the vertical net force is zero.
The two vertical forces must have equal magnitudes.
Calculate the weight 4 × 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no vertical acceleration, the support force balances the weight: mg = 4 × 10 = 40 N.

questions.onCorrect: 40 N. At rest the net force is zero, so the support force equals the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass. The support force must match the weight, which is mg.
Gravity is pulling down, so something must be pushing up to keep the object at rest.

questions.prompt: A support accelerates a 4 kg object upward at 2 m/s². Only support and weight act, and g = 10 m/s². Find the support force in newtons.
hints: The support has to balance the weight and also give a net upward force.
Use support force = m(g + a).
Add g and the acceleration, then multiply by the mass.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Support force − mg = ma, so the support force = 4 × (10 + 2) = 48 N.

questions.onCorrect: 48 N. The support carries the weight and supplies extra force to accelerate the object upward.

misconceptions.feedback: That only balances the weight. The object is also accelerating upward, which needs more.
That is the extra force for the acceleration alone. The support also carries the weight.

questions.prompt: A 7 kg object is in a field where g = 9.8 m/s². Find its weight magnitude in newtons.
hints: Use the given value of g rather than rounding it to 10.
Multiply mass by gravitational acceleration.
Calculate 7 × 9.8.
questions.onCorrect: 68.6 N. Use the g you are given: weight is mass times g.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds g to 10. The question gives 9.8, so use it.
That divides the mass by g. Weight is mass times g.

questions.prompt: An object on a support moves downward at a constant velocity. Only its weight and the support force act. How does the support force compare with the weight?
hints: Downward velocity does not imply downward acceleration.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Constant velocity gives zero acceleration, so the support and weight balance.

questions.onCorrect: Equal. Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the support balances the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: A smaller support force would leave a net downward force and the object would speed up downward.
A larger support force would give a net upward force and the object would slow down.

questions.prompt: What is the weight of a 6 kg bag, in newtons? Take g = 10 N per kilogram.
hints: How much pull is there on one kilogram?
Each kilogram has its own 10 N.
Count the kilograms and multiply.
questions.onCorrect: 60 N. Weight is the pull on each kilogram times the number of kilograms: W = mg.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. Each kilogram gets its own 10 N, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object weighs 30 N on Earth. On a planet where g = 4 m/s², what does it weigh, in newtons?
hints: Does the 3 kg change when the object moves?
Weight is mass times g for the new planet.
Multiply the mass by the new g.
questions.onCorrect: 12 N. The mass is still 3 kg. Only g changed, so the weight did.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the weight on Earth. The new planet has a different g.
That adds the mass and g. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A 7 kg box rests on a shelf. Only its weight and the shelf's upward force act, with g = 10 m/s². What is the upward force from the shelf, in newtons?
hints: Is the box accelerating?
Then the net force is zero.
The shelf force must match the weight.
questions.onCorrect: 70 N. With no acceleration, the support force equals the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: The box is not falling, so something is holding it up.
That is the mass. The force is mass times g.

questions.prompt: Why must the support force be larger than the weight here?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: The net force must point upward to give an upward acceleration.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The net force must point upward to give an upward acceleration.

choices.label: The net force must point upward to give an upward acceleration.
The object gets heavier when it moves.
Gravity switches off in a lift.

questions.onCorrect: Net force is support minus weight. For an upward acceleration it has to be positive.

misconceptions.feedback: The weight stays mg. It is the support that changes.
Gravity keeps pulling. The support has to do more than balance it.

questions.prompt: A 6 kg load in a lift accelerates downward at 3 m/s². Only its weight and the support force act, with g = 10 m/s². What is the support force, in newtons?
hints: Upward is positive, so the acceleration is negative.
Use support force = m(g + a) with a negative.
Take the acceleration off g, then multiply by the mass.
questions.onCorrect: 42 N. The load accelerates down, so the support force is less than the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: That only balances the weight. The load is accelerating downward, so the support gives less than that.
That treats the acceleration as upward. It points down, so it reduces the support force.
